extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate and advanced-competition mathematics students / readers of Math.StackExchange looking for solution sketches
extracted.subtask_description: Sketching concise, correct proofs and solution outlines for a wide range of undergraduate-level (and competition-level) problems in algebra, topology, analysis, and number theory; emphasizes common techniques, pitfalls, and short constructive arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify union is a proper upper bound when applying Zorn's lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: When using Zorn's lemma one typically takes unions of chains to produce upper bounds; be sure to verify that the union is a proper object in the poset (i.e. satisfies the required property).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit reminder in solutions: 'using a union trick to verify the condition; be sure to verify that the union is proper!'. Anti-pattern: applying Zorn's lemma without checking the union stays inside the family being considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary heavy machinery when hypotheses forbid its use
rubrics_metrics.description: If hypotheses already rule out the obstruction that a theorem addresses, you do not need the theorem (e.g. if there are no ascending infinite chains, you need not invoke Zorn's lemma).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: choose the simplest appropriate tool rather than overcomplicating the proof with unnecessary abstract theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove maximality of an ideal by showing quotient is a finite integral domain
rubrics_metrics.description: If R/I is finite and an integral domain, then R/I is a field, so I is maximal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in text: show R/I has finitely many elements (by reducing representatives modulo some nonzero integer), then use integrality to conclude field. Useful pattern: reduce to counting/size arguments for algebraic maximality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct fixed points via iteration and geometric contraction bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove existence of a fixed point for a contraction-like map, start with any x0, iterate xn+1 = T(xn), show the iterates satisfy a geometric decay bound making them Cauchy, use completeness to get a limit, and continuity to show the limit is fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example used r = 0.999 and c = d(x0,x1) to show d(xM,xN) ≤ (r^M)/(1−r)·c → 0. Also note uniqueness of fixed point often follows immediately from contraction property by contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish boundedness from total boundedness/compactness carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric space can be bounded but not totally bounded; check the definitions directly (e.g. show you cannot cover the space by finitely many ε-balls for some ε).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: space M with distances ≤1 is bounded but not totally bounded since it cannot be covered by finitely many 1/2-neighborhoods. Remember: completeness + total boundedness ⇒ compactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the identity map to show homeomorphism when metrics/topologies match
rubrics_metrics.description: If two metric/topological spaces have the same underlying set with different metrics/topologies, showing the identity map is continuous both ways proves a homeomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text: 'The identity map (!) is a homeomorphism M ∼= R since it is continuous.' Use identity when topology change is only by a metrically equivalent description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagonal (subsequence) argument for compactness in product spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a sequence in X×Y has a convergent subsequence, first take a subsequence whose X-components converge, then from the corresponding Y-components extract a convergent subsequence, producing a diagonal subsequence in X×Y converging to (x,y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning/anti-pattern: you cannot extract unrelated subsequences from X and Y independently and expect them to pair up; you must filter Y via the subsequence chosen on X.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build unbounded continuous functions from noncompact sequences via disjoint bump functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a sequence without convergent subsequence, select disjoint small balls around each point and define local bump functions that add up to an unbounded continuous function; use it to modify the metric to make the space unbounded while homeomorphic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction in text defines F(x) to be (ri − d(x,ai)) on Ci and 0 outside; then set new metric d'(x,y)=d(x,y)+|F(x)−F(y)| to get an unbounded metric homeomorphic to original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Cantor intersection theorem for nested closed sets with vanishing radii
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a nested sequence of nonempty compact (or closed) sets whose diameters (or radii) tend to zero, then their intersection is nonempty (often a single point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to contradict existence of infinite partition into disjoint circles by showing nested closed disks' radii approach zero forcing a common point in all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use coloring and maximal/minimal-by-inclusion arguments in topological partition proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Color regions/curves according to membership and analyze the family of colored sets ordered by inclusion to obtain closed/open descriptions or find maximal/minimal elements leading to contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: color circles magenta/cyan/neon and argue magenta circles are totally ordered by inclusion; consider whether there exists a maximal magenta circle to derive structure of the magenta set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank–nullity as a primary tool to compare injectivity/surjectivity in finite dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: For linear maps between finite-dimensional vector spaces, use the rank-nullity theorem to deduce impossibility or possibility of injective/surjective maps based on dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly: e.g. any injective map V→W forces dim V ≤ dim W; if dims equal, injective ⇔ surjective; counterexamples by zero map when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute trace or determinant by choosing a convenient basis (Jordan form, orthonormal basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: To compute trace or reason about eigenvalues, pick a basis (e.g., Jordan form, orthonormal basis) that makes the matrix form simple so diagonal entries/eigenvalues are explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace = sum of eigenvalues in any basis; choose Jordan form to read off diagonal eigenvalues directly. For inner-product-compatible diagonalization, use orthonormal eigenbasis and Lagrange interpolation to match polynomial constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit Cayley–Hamilton and minimal polynomial relations to relate M^k to lower powers
rubrics_metrics.description: If a matrix satisfies a polynomial relation (e.g., its characteristic polynomial), express high powers M^k as linear combinations of lower powers to deduce constraints on eigenvalues or matrix entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to show M^k = cM + dI and deduce eigenvalue symmetries (e.g., eigenvalues negatives of each other) or impossibility of certain patterns unless parameters vanish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parity/modular reductions on determinants to deduce invertibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce a determinant computation modulo a small prime (e.g., mod 2) to compute parity of determinant and deduce whether matrix is invertible over Z or fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show det M (mod 2) equals number of derangements, which is odd, hence det M is odd and invertible over Z.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group and pair series terms strategically to show Cauchy/absolute convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: When establishing convergence/Cauchyness of alternating or rearranged series, group terms cleverly to bound tails by a single early term or otherwise force Cauchy property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bounding alternating tail by aM via pairing differences; technique applies to show partial sums form a Cauchy sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summation by parts / Abel-type arguments to handle series of monotone×bounded sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: To show convergence of ∑ a_n b_n when (a_n) are partial-sum-type monotone bounded and (b_n) monotone to 0, rewrite the sum and bound tails using uniform bounds on partial sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text applies decomposition and bounding of tails with ε by choosing K where bn-tail small and then bounding contribution of initial xj using total mass A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove limits of monotone bounded real recurrences by monotone-limits substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: If a real sequence defined recursively is monotone and bounded, it converges; substitute the limit into the recurrence to determine possible limiting values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: xn+1 = log(exn − xn) shown decreasing and nonnegative, therefore limit L; deduce L by passing to limit in defining relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Taylor series / nonvanishing leading coefficient to rule out accumulation of zeros
rubrics_metrics.description: If an analytic function has infinitely many distinct zeros accumulating at a point, the Taylor series at that point must be identically zero; a nonzero leading coefficient contradicts this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in proof by contradiction: assume distinct zeros converge to z, expand f about z, nonzero lowest coefficient gives neighborhood where f ≠ 0, contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nullstellensatz trick: add auxiliary variable to force empty zero locus and 'clear denominators'
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a polynomial f lies in the radical of an ideal I, consider the ideal I' = (I, x_{n+1} f − 1) in the extended polynomial ring; if V(I') = ∅ then 1 ∈ I', yielding an algebraic relation expressing a power of f in I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic algebraic-geometry technique used to prove membership in radical: produce combination 1 = Σ gi fi + g_{m+1}(x_{n+1} f − 1) and clear x_{n+1} to get f^N ∈ I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid taking independent convergent subsequences of coordinates in product sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When trying to extract a convergent subsequence from a sequence in a product space, you must extract subsequent subsequences in a filtered manner (use diagonal argument) rather than extracting unrelated convergent subsequences for coordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly flagged as a common mistake in the product-compactness proof: independent subsequences for xn and yn may correspond to different index sets and not give a convergent subsequence in the product.
